A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BARL research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task experiments in Section 6 and mathematical reasoning results, ablations, and additional model experiments in Section 7 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains the original synthetic and mathematical reasoning experiments, including benchmark scores, training curves, and appendix analyses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains candidate-answer sampling, answer-defined MDP hypotheses, posterior weighting using reward consistency, and policy-gradient updates. The data-conditioned objective and more general reward-scorer notation revise the formulation without establishing a different implemented training or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use Big-Math training, the synthetic triplet task, and evaluation on GSM8K, MATH, CollegeMath, OlympiadBench, AIME 2024, and AMC 2023. AIME and AMC enter v2's main table but were already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: GRPO and the MRT-derived Progress baseline remain the main comparators. Base-model comparisons, length-controlled GRPO, and the comparator membership in appendix experiments are retained. Newly cited related methods are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Table 1's Average changes from four benchmarks to six by including AIME and AMC, changing the aggregate evaluation metric. Model configurations, training budgets, response limits, and decoding procedures otherwise remain the same; the PDFs do not establish experimental reruns.

E4.justification: The candidate-set comparison, token-efficiency analysis, reflection-frequency analysis, Bayesian-value analysis, and length-controlled GRPO experiment are retained. Appendix B also retains the Llama-3.2-3B experiment, sampling-only analysis, and unsuccessful ensemble attempts without new analytical evidence.

E5.justification: Section 7.2 and Table 1 change uncertainty reporting from standard deviation to standard error while retaining three training seeds. Most existing uncertainty values remain identical. Appendix B.1 newly specifies a common random seed for its curves; no increase in run counts is stated.

E6.justification: Six existing Table 1 accuracy entries change, including Qwen-1.5B BARL on GSM8K from 86.0 to 85.8 and GRPO on OlympiadBench from 33.4 to 31.6. v2 adds AIME/AMC mean-and-error summaries. Its six-benchmark averages are not directly comparable with v1's four-benchmark averages; the empirical plots retain their results.

T1.justification: v2 introduces formal uncertainty-adaptive and reflective-exploration definitions, an explicit training-data posterior objective, and a new adaptive-optimality theorem. Appendix A adds proofs using an epistemic POMDP definition and objective-equivalence lemma. v1's gap theorem becomes Theorem 4.3 with a revised proof, while its telescoping reward-shaping argument is removed.

C1.justification: The central BARL contribution and performance claims remain. v2 sharpens reflection into belief-dependent uncertainty adaptation, explicitly claims optimal adaptive-policy existence, and restates the exponential-in-depth advantage as an arbitrarily large Bayes-return gap.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies adaptive optimality as structural and potentially compatible with a Markovian policy. It removes v1's infinite-horizon discussion and specific AIME/AMC training-length caveat, attributes stylistic reflections to pretraining, and changes the ensemble-failure explanation from shared parameters to insufficient trainable parameters.

D1.justification: v2 removes the statement identifying OpenRLHF as the implementation framework and the specific BLoB reference for the unsuccessful Bayesian LoRA implementation. The code link and principal experimental hyperparameters remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds comparisons with Bayesian LLM exploration work by Arumugam and Griffiths and by Dwaracherla and colleagues, distinguishing direct policy fine-tuning from external exploration or data collection. Section 4 adds connections to meta-RL and continual learning. Several references are also removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, theoretical discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. The narrative is reorganized around training versus deployment and uncertainty adaptation, with new definition and proof subsections and widespread terminology revisions.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains two benchmark columns, shorter labels, and denser formatting. Figures 1–3 are resized, repositioned, or relabeled, including Test-to-Eval terminology. The empirical charts are retained, with surrounding text and captions reflowed.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies the deployment formulation, qualifies adaptive optimality, and consolidates benchmark reporting. However, condition (2) of its new Definition 3.2 appears to force identical policies at equal latent states, conflicting with the definition's required action-distribution difference. Table 1 also relabels largely unchanged uncertainty values from standard deviation to standard error without explanation. These theoretical and reporting issues prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
